title: Updating twice
summary: Two pieces of evidence: multiply two likelihood ratios, check it with counts, and see when that is allowed.

blocks.title: A second word
blocks.why: A second piece of evidence has its own ratio. You compute it exactly as the first.
blocks.prompt: After the word “free” the odds of spam are 3. Now see the word “winner”, in $\frac{1}{2}$ of spam and $\frac{1}{10}$ of ham. Find its likelihood ratio.

slips.say: That is flipped. Spam on top.
That subtracts the rates. A ratio divides.

blocks.title: Odds after both words
blocks.why: Updating twice is multiplying twice. Order does not matter.
blocks.prompt: $P(\text{spam}) = \frac{1}{5}$. “free” has likelihood ratio 12 and “winner” has 5. Find the odds of spam after both words: prior odds times both ratios.

slips.say: That adds the odds of 3 and the ratio 5. Updates multiply.
That is $12 \times 5$ with the prior odds $\frac{1}{4}$ left out.

hints: Prior odds first: spam to ham.

blocks.title: Probability after both
blocks.why: Odds above 1 mean more likely than not.
blocks.prompt: After both words, the odds of spam are 15. Find $P(\text{spam})$ using $P = \frac{\text{odds}}{1 + \text{odds}}$. Give a fraction.

slips.say: That is the ham share. Spam is the 15.
That is after “free” alone. Use odds 15.

hints: That is 15 out of how many?

blocks.title: Check with counts
blocks.why: Two ways to one answer is how you trust a method.
blocks.prompt: Out of 1,000 emails, 800 are ham. Ham has “free” in $\frac{1}{20}$ and “winner” in $\frac{1}{10}$, and the two words appear independently within ham. How many ham emails have both words?

slips.say: That is ham with “free” only. Then take $\frac{1}{10}$ of those.
That is ham with “winner” only ($800 \times \frac{1}{10}$). Take $\frac{1}{20}$ of those.

hints: Take $\frac{1}{20}$ of the 800, then $\frac{1}{10}$ of that.
blocks.solution: Spam with both: $200 \times \frac{3}{5} \times \frac{1}{2} = 60$. So $\frac{60}{60 + 4} = \frac{15}{16}$, matching the odds method.

blocks.title: When may you multiply ratios?
blocks.why: Multiplying ratios is only valid under one condition. Spam filters rely on it, often wrongly.
blocks.prompt: We multiplied the ratios 12 (“free”) and 5 (“winner”). Which assumption makes that correct?

options.text: Given the email is spam (and given it is ham), the two words occur independently.
options.say: Right. The rates $\frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{20}\cdot\frac{1}{10}$ multiply only if, within each class, one word tells you nothing about the other.

options.text: Across all emails, the two words are independent of each other.
options.say: Not this one. They are usually not: both are more common in spam, so across all emails seeing one makes the other likelier.

options.text: Each word has a likelihood ratio above 1.
options.say: Not this one. That is true here and says both point to spam, but it does not make the product valid.

options.text: The prior probability of spam is small.
options.say: Not this one. The prior is only the starting odds. It plays no part in whether ratios multiply.

blocks.hint: The products are of rates measured inside one group.
blocks.solution: Multiplying ratios assumes independence within each class. It is called naive Bayes.

blocks.title: Two positive tests
blocks.why: The medical test again: how much does a second, independent positive help?
blocks.prompt: 1% of people are sick. A test is positive for 90% of the sick and 5% of the healthy. Someone has two positive results from independent repeats (independent given sick or healthy). Find $P(\text{sick})$. Give a fraction.

slips.say: That counts one positive. Multiply by the ratio 18 a second time.
That is the odds. Convert with $\frac{\text{odds}}{1 + \text{odds}}$.

blocks.solution: Two positives take $\frac{2}{13}$ to $\frac{36}{47}$, about 77%. Run the same sample twice and the errors repeat, so the repeats are not independent and the multiplication would be wrong.
